mcqs.question: Why does marking Money final matter for its immutability guarantee?
options: Without it, a subclass could override plus() to mutate this instead of returning a new instance, silently breaking every caller relying on Money being immutable
Because final classes are automatically thread-safe regardless of their fields
Because final is required for any class with a private field
Because it prevents Money from being passed as a method argument
mcqs.explanation: final closes the loophole where a subclass could quietly reintroduce mutation. final alone doesn't guarantee thread safety on its own, isn't required for private fields, and has no effect on passing instances as arguments.

mcqs.question: How do you keep a final class from hurting testability?
options: Avoid final entirely on any class that might ever need a test double
Depend on an interface in the code under test, rather than the concrete final class, and provide a real or fake implementation of that interface for tests
Use reflection to bypass the final modifier during tests
Mark the test class itself final to match
mcqs.explanation: Depending on an abstraction rather than the concrete final class moves the testing seam to the interface, so final on the implementation costs nothing there. Reflection hacks and blanket avoidance of final aren't the pattern this follow-up is testing for.

mcqs.question: What's the honest framing of final's runtime/JIT benefit, per this follow-up?
options: It's the primary reason to mark a class final — performance should drive the decision
There is no runtime benefit at all; it's purely a design-time signal
It's a real secondary benefit (devirtualization) that follows naturally from a correctness-driven decision — not a justification for marking something final on its own
It only applies to classes with more than one subclass
mcqs.explanation: Devirtualization is a genuine but secondary benefit that rides along with a design decision made for correctness reasons. Chasing performance alone gets the reasoning backwards, but claiming zero runtime benefit is also inaccurate, and the benefit has nothing to do with subclass count.

mcqs.question: Why is sealing a Handler hierarchy wrong when third-party plugins are expected to add new handler types?
options: Because sealed classes cannot have more than three subtypes
Because plugins can never implement Java interfaces, only extend classes
Because sealed hierarchies are deprecated in favor of final
sealed enumerates every allowed subtype at compile time in the same codebase, which is fundamentally incompatible with letting outside code add new subtypes
mcqs.explanation: sealed's whole point is a compile-time-known, closed set of subtypes in the same codebase, which directly conflicts with an open plugin extension point. There's no subtype-count limit, plugins can implement interfaces fine, and sealed isn't deprecated.
